name: Self-Determination Theory
statement: People thrive when their needs for autonomy, competence, and relatedness are met, and act best from genuine interest.
meaning: Self-determination theory is a broad theory of human motivation and personality developed by the psychologists Edward Deci and Richard Ryan, growing out of Deci's research in the early 1970s and consolidated notably in their 1985 book and later work. It concerns the degree to which people's behavior is self-motivated and self-determined rather than controlled by external pressures. A central distinction is between intrinsic motivation, doing something because it is inherently interesting or enjoyable, and extrinsic motivation, doing something for a separable outcome such as a reward or to avoid punishment. The theory holds that people function and flourish best when they act out of intrinsic motivation or well-internalized values, and that this depends on the satisfaction of three basic psychological needs: autonomy, the sense of acting from one's own volition; competence, the sense of being effective and capable; and relatedness, the sense of being connected to and cared for by others. When social environments support these needs, people show higher-quality motivation, better performance, and greater well-being; when environments thwart them, motivation and well-being suffer. A well-known related finding is that offering external rewards for an already interesting activity can undermine intrinsic motivation. Self-determination theory is one of the most influential and empirically supported theories of motivation.
mechanism: Self-determination theory explains motivation through the interplay of the type of motivation and the satisfaction of basic psychological needs. Motivation is not simply a matter of how much a person is driven but of what kind of drive is at work. Intrinsic motivation, arising when an activity is interesting or enjoyable in itself, tends to produce engagement, persistence, creativity, and well-being. Extrinsic motivation, driven by outcomes separate from the activity, varies in quality depending on how fully the reason has been internalized, from feeling externally controlled to acting from personally endorsed values. The theory holds that whether motivation is high-quality and whether a person flourishes depends on the satisfaction of three innate needs. Autonomy is the need to feel that one's actions are self-chosen and volitional rather than coerced; competence is the need to feel effective and capable of mastering challenges; and relatedness is the need to feel connected to and valued by others. Environments that support these needs, by offering choice, meaningful feedback, and warmth, foster intrinsic motivation and well-being, while controlling or isolating environments undermine them. A striking demonstration is the undermining or overjustification effect: rewarding people for an activity they already find intrinsically interesting can reduce their later intrinsic interest, because the reward is experienced as controlling and shifts the perceived reason for acting.

examples.text: People show higher-quality motivation and well-being when their needs for autonomy, competence, and relatedness are satisfied.
Doing something for its own interest is intrinsic motivation, while doing it for a reward or to avoid punishment is extrinsic.
Rewarding people for an activity they already enjoy can reduce their intrinsic motivation for it, as Deci's early experiments showed.

whyItMatters: Self-determination theory is one of the most influential and empirically well-supported theories of human motivation, reshaping how psychologists and practitioners understand what makes people engaged, persistent, and fulfilled. By distinguishing the quality of motivation, not just its quantity, and by identifying autonomy, competence, and relatedness as basic psychological needs whose satisfaction underlies healthy motivation and well-being, the theory offers a powerful framework that applies across education, work, health, sport, and parenting. Its insight that supporting people's autonomy and sense of competence fosters better outcomes than controlling them has informed teaching that nurtures interest rather than relying on rewards and punishments, management that motivates through meaning and choice, and healthcare that helps patients internalize the reasons for behavior change. Its finding that external rewards can undermine intrinsic motivation challenged simple behaviorist assumptions and has practical implications for how incentives are used. Backed by a large body of experimental and applied research, self-determination theory has become a central account of motivation in contemporary psychology. As the theory that explains how genuine, self-determined motivation arises and why it matters, it is foundational to the study of human motivation and flourishing.

limits: Self-determination theory is strongly supported, but a few points warrant care. It is an umbrella framework made up of several sub-theories, so a short summary of its needs and distinctions necessarily simplifies a more elaborate structure. The universality of the three basic needs, especially autonomy, has been debated, with some arguing that its emphasis reflects individualistic Western values and that autonomy is expressed differently in more collectivist cultures, though proponents respond that the need for volition, properly understood, appears across cultures. The undermining effect of rewards on intrinsic motivation, while robust, is nuanced, since not all rewards undermine motivation equally, and unexpected or informational rewards can differ from expected controlling ones. So self-determination theory robustly explains high-quality motivation through autonomy, competence, and relatedness, understood as a rich framework whose cross-cultural claims and reward effects carry real nuance.
misreadings: Self-determination theory does not say all extrinsic motivation is bad; extrinsic motivation varies in quality depending on how well its reasons are internalized, and well-internalized values support flourishing. It does not claim rewards always undermine motivation, since the undermining effect is specific to controlling rewards for already-interesting activities, and informational rewards can differ. And its emphasis on autonomy is not simply a Western bias, though its cross-cultural expression is debated, so treating all extrinsic motivation as harmful, all rewards as undermining, or autonomy as merely a Western value, misreads a well-supported but nuanced theory of motivation.
origin: A theory of human motivation developed by the psychologists Edward Deci and Richard Ryan from the early 1970s and consolidated in their 1985 book, centered on intrinsic motivation and the basic needs for autonomy, competence, and relatedness.
